source_refs.note: Topic 14.7 with Example 14.5 and the note (PDF 31-35); Figs 14.10 and 14.11 redrawn. Example 14.5 is solved from the mean position and the book's version is reported in a warning; flagged for review. The check question is added.

blocks.text: A body executing S.H.M. has both potential energy, because of its displacement from the mean position, and kinetic energy, because of its velocity. These energies change during the oscillation, but in the absence of friction the total energy at any instant stays constant.

For a mass on a spring (Fig 14.10), the restoring force is zero at x = 0 and kxo at x = xo, so its average value while stretching from O to xo is Fav = (0 + kxo)/2 = (1/2) kxo. The work done in stretching the spring to xo is W = Fav x xo = (1/2) kxo^2, stored as elastic potential energy. At any displacement x, P.E. = (1/2) kx^2 (14.22); it is zero at x = 0 and maximum at x = +/- xo: (P.E.)max = (1/2) kxo^2 (14.23).

blocks.alt: Three identical springs hang from a ceiling with a mass m on each. The first mass rests at the mean position O (x = 0). The second is pulled down to x = +xo and the restoring force F acts upward. The third is pushed up to x = -xo and F acts downward. A panel lists: F = -kx; F = 0 at x = 0; F = kxo at x = +-xo; average force (1/2) kxo; work done (1/2) kxo squared; P.E. = (1/2) kx squared, maximum (1/2) kxo squared.
blocks.caption: A mass on a spring at the mean position and at the two extreme positions (original diagram after Fig 14.10).
blocks.long_description: The restoring force grows from zero at O to kxo at an extreme position, so the average force over the stretch is (1/2) kxo and the work done is (1/2) kxo squared. This work is stored as elastic potential energy, which is greatest at the extremes and zero at the mean position.

blocks.text: The speed at displacement x is v = w square root of (xo^2 - x^2) = square root of [(k/m)(xo^2 - x^2)] (14.24), with the maximum v_max = square root of (k/m) xo at x = 0 (14.25). So K.E. = (1/2) mv^2 = (1/2) k(xo^2 - x^2) (14.26). At the mean position P.E. is zero and the total energy is all kinetic: T.E. = (K.E.)max = (1/2) kxo^2 (14.27). At any displacement, T.E. = K.E. + P.E. = (1/2) k(xo^2 - x^2) + (1/2) kx^2 = (1/2) kxo^2 (14.28). Since k = m w^2, T.E. = (1/2) m w^2 xo^2 (14.29).

So the total energy of a mass-spring system is constant and directly proportional to the square of the amplitude. This conservation of energy holds for all bodies executing S.H.M. When K.E. is maximum the mass is passing through the centre of oscillation and P.E. is zero; when P.E. is maximum the mass is at an extreme and K.E. is zero. The energy passes back and forth between K.E. and P.E., but their sum stays constant (Fig 14.11).

blocks.alt: Graph of energy against displacement from -xo to +xo. A blue upward parabola, P.E. = (1/2)kx^2, is zero at the centre and highest at the ends. A red downward parabola, K.E. = (1/2)k(xo^2 - x^2), is highest at the centre and zero at the ends. A dashed purple horizontal line, total = (1/2)kxo^2, touches both curves at their maxima. The curves cross halfway up.
blocks.caption: Kinetic, potential and total energy in S.H.M. (original graph after Fig 14.11).
blocks.long_description: At every displacement the red and blue heights add up to the dashed line: energy only changes form between kinetic and potential.

blocks.text: A body of mass 0.010 kg executes S.H.M. with a period of 6 s. One second after it has passed its mean position, its speed is 0.06 m s^-1. Find its kinetic energy, potential energy and total energy. Solution: w = 2 pi / T = 2 pi / 6 = pi/3 rad s^-1, about 1.047 rad s^-1. K.E. = (1/2) mv^2 = (1/2)(0.010)(0.06)^2 = 1.8 x 10^-5 J. Measuring time from the mean position, x = xo sin(wt) and v = xo w cos(wt). At t = 1 s, wt = pi/3 and cos(pi/3) = 0.5, so 0.06 = xo (1.047)(0.5) and xo = 0.115 m. Total energy E = (1/2) m w^2 xo^2 = (1/2)(0.010)(1.047)^2(0.115)^2 = 7.2 x 10^-5 J. P.E. = E - K.E. = 7.2 x 10^-5 - 1.8 x 10^-5 = 5.4 x 10^-5 J. (Check: x = xo sin(pi/3) = 0.099 m and (1/2) m w^2 x^2 = 5.4 x 10^-5 J.)
